attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in his own post, stated as his belief.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the statement: current systems are better than an earlier generation, and that doesn't mean anything is 'over'. The 'over' part is a judgement with no measurable endpoint.

contract.note: Reading 'better' as broader overall competence than pre-LLM chatbots is an ordinary, fair reading. Imitation rates alone don't count. The 'over' clause can't be tested. The result depends on the evaluator's reading of 'better'.

evidence.note: A May 2024 study: GPT-4 beat ELIZA on human-judgement rate. This shows only an improvement in imitation, from an earlier period. It does not measure broad competence and does not compare against Goostman.
The March 2025 study treats humanlikeness as separate from intelligence. It gives no broad capability comparison with the earlier generation.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no comparable evaluation of broad competence between current systems and Goostman-era chatbots. It shows only gains in imitation, which the contract rules out as enough. The 'nothing is over' part is a judgement that can't be tested. The evidence doesn't settle the measurable part.

attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in the closing section of his post.

semantics.note: Both parts are kept: great progress in mimicry since 2014, and a lot still missing in reasoning, planning and common sense.

contract.note: Reading 'a lot missing' as large gaps against human baselines around early 2025 is an ordinary, fair reading. The support condition accepts gaps in reasoning, planning or common sense.

evidence.note: A controlled three-party Turing test in March 2025: GPT-4.5 with a persona prompt was picked as human 73% of the time. That is strong evidence of progress in mimicry.
When ARC-AGI-2 launched in March 2025, frontier models scored about 1–4% against a human-panel baseline of 60%. That is a large reasoning gap.
September 2024: o1 was still far from saturating PlanBench despite big gains. This is evidence of a planning gap within the target period.
o3 matched human performance on ARC-AGI-1 in December 2024. This weakly cuts against how big the gap is, but one benchmark is not broad parity.

reviews.rationale: Mimicry clearly improved: the first three-party Turing-test pass. Evaluations from around the post date show large gaps against humans on new reasoning tasks (ARC-AGI-2) and on planning (PlanBench). o3's human-level ARC-AGI-1 score is limited counterevidence, not broad parity. There is no direct common-sense benchmark, but the contract's 'or' condition is met.

attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words describing the Jones & Bergen paper.

semantics.note: The no-persona condition is kept. 'ChatGPT' is ambiguous: GPT-4o was ChatGPT's default model, while GPT-4.5 is the model discussed nearby.

contract.note: The contract doesn't settle which model is meant, and the result depends on it. Its rule that a different 'out-of-the-box setup' counts as a contradiction is unfair: Marcus explicitly glossed the phrase as the paper's no-persona condition.

evidence.note: UCSD's write-up of the March 2025 results (published before the evaluation date): ELIZA was picked as human 23% of the time vs GPT-4o's 21%. This supports the GPT-4o reading.
The original paper gives GPT-4.5 without a persona 36%, above ELIZA's 23%, which contradicts the GPT-4.5 reading. The same section lists GPT-4o without a persona at 21% vs ELIZA 23%.

reviews.rationale: Read as GPT-4o (ChatGPT's default model, tested only without a persona), the claim holds: 21% vs ELIZA's 23%, a numerical gap that wasn't statistically significant. Read as GPT-4.5 without a persona, it fails: 36% vs 23%. Marcus didn't say which model he meant, so the result splits by reading.

attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition matches: those who could afford the comprehension challenge spend on scaling instead. 'Prefer' is a claim about motive, read here through where the spending goes.

contract.note: Reading 'prefer' as revealed preference in early-2025 spending is ordinary and fair. Data-center capital spending is an imperfect stand-in for research dollars, since it also serves products.

evidence.note: January 2025: the Stargate plan put up to $500B into data-center compute for OpenAI and partners. Clear evidence of spending on scaling.
OpenAI's own statement, quoted in the press, says the extra compute is for training leading models. This is a company disclosure, not an independent finding.
January 2025: Microsoft planned $80B+ on AI data centers for FY2025. This fits the picture of where the money went, though some of it serves customers and products.

reviews.rationale: Early-2025 reports show the best-funded AI players committing hundreds of billions to compute and model training. The packet shows no lab funding a comprehension-challenge-style test, and no evidence meets the contradiction condition. The caveats: capital spending is not purely research, and the comparison with funding the test is qualitative.
